title: Being loved
hook: receiving love is part of holiness too
tomorrow: what can happen in the five minutes before Mass even starts?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb because the people he loved were weeping. When words run out, the line was just stay.

Someone offers to pay, and you're already reaching for your card. Someone asks how you are, and you say fine and turn the question around. Being on the receiving end takes practice. At the Last Supper, Jesus takes off his outer garment, ties a towel around himself, pours water into a basin and starts washing his friends' feet. When he reaches Peter, Peter stops him. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Thou shalt never wash my feet."
screen: `I'VE GOT IT. I'M FINE.` → `A TOWEL AND A BASIN.` → `NEVER MY FEET.`

segments.voice: So why refuse? Peter can't bear to see his teacher kneeling at his dusty feet. It sounds like humility. Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." Being loved isn't optional; it's the way in. So Peter swings the other way: not only my feet, but my hands and my head. Then Jesus says that once they've been served, they're to do the same for one another. Receiving comes first. John's first letter puts the order plainly: "Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us." A neighbor tradition knows this lesson by heart. In Jewish practice, after a burial, mourners sitting shiva don't make their own first meal. Neighbors bring it, the meal of condolence, called the seudat havra'ah, and the Talmud and later Jewish law say the mourner shouldn't eat his own bread at that meal. The mourner's part, for once, is simply to be fed. That's shared ground: both traditions count receiving care as part of a holy life, not a failure at it. And an honest difference: Catholics see the deepest picture in Jesus, whom they believe is God made flesh, kneeling at Peter's feet. Judaism doesn't hold that God took flesh; its meal is a commandment neighbors keep for one another.
screen: `PETER SAYS NO.` · `NO PART WITH ME.` · `GOD FIRST HATH LOVED US.` · `THE MEAL OF CONDOLENCE.` · then, large: `LET YOURSELF BE LOVED.`

segments.voice: Find one thing near you that someone else made, gave or fixed for you: a mug, a sweater, a note, the meal you just ate. Hold it or look at it for a while, and let yourself stay on the receiving end, without planning how to pay it back. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person behind it.
Being loved. Letting yourself receive care, from God and from people, without earning it first. Today's word.
Hold onto this: let yourself be loved, the way Peter finally held out his feet. That's the day, and the week is nearly done.

chat.meaning: Jesus told Peter that being served was part of having a share with him. Receiving love isn't a weakness; in John's letter it comes first.

The meal of condolence (seudat havra'ah): Moed Katan 27b and Shulchan Aruch YD 378:1 (a mourner may not eat of his own bread at the first meal after the burial; neighbors provide it). Shared ground: receiving care as part of a holy life. Honest difference: Catholics see it in Jesus, believed to be God made flesh; Judaism does not hold that God took flesh, and the meal is a commandment between neighbors.
